solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Mia Klein periodically visited country (4)

indicatorNotes.periodically: at regular intervals: take every other letter

annotation.surface: A woman named Mia Klein goes abroad now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: Mia Klein is nobody; the name exists only to supply letters. Count the space as nothing: M, A, L, I are the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Mali is one of many countries, a landlocked state in West Africa.

entries.clue: Smuggle in a cutting implement (6)

indicatorNotes.in: one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: a = per, as in 'ten pounds a head'
to run guns or drugs is to smuggle them

annotation.surface: Someone sneaks a blade past customs.
annotation.walkthrough: The little word 'a' does real work here: 'a' and 'per' are interchangeable in prices, so it supplies PER to hold RUN.
annotation.definitionFit: A pruner is a tool for cutting back plants.

entries.clue: Good law easing supply for Govan native (10)

indicatorNotes.supply: read as the adverb of 'supple': bendily, so the letters are bent into a new order

blocks.note: G = good, the standard abbreviation, rearranged along with the rest

annotation.surface: A kinder law is brought in to help a man from Glasgow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun, as in provision, but it is the adverb 'supply' (in a supple way). Govan is a district of Glasgow on the Clyde.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone born in Govan is born in Glasgow, so is a Glaswegian.

entries.clue: Drink in sailor’s world? (6)

blocks.note: AB = able seaman, a sailor, plus the 's
the orb = the globe, the world

annotation.surface: A question about what a sailor gets to drink in his world.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drink in' reads as drinking inside somewhere, but it is one phrasal verb, meaning to take in eagerly.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: taking in a view or a lecture eagerly is soaking it up.

entries.clue: Cook hake endlessly and broil some greens (8)

indicatorNotes.Cook: to cook is to work ingredients into something new
indicatorNotes.endlessly: without its end: drop the final letter

annotation.surface: A kitchen instruction: prepare the fish and grill some vegetables.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as two separate cooking jobs, but 'cook' works on the fish and 'broil' together, and 'broil' is only letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Kohlrabi is a cabbage-family vegetable, so it counts as some greens.

entries.clue: Saint Christopher’s parody (4)

blocks.note: Kit is a pet form of Christopher; the 's is 'has', joining to the definition

annotation.surface: A reference to a mocking piece about St Christopher.
annotation.walkthrough: Saint Christopher looks like one name, the patron of travellers, but it splits into S and a nickname for Christopher.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a short comic sketch mocking something is a parody.

entries.clue: Hot tub with two males excited little fellow (3,5)

indicatorNotes.excited: stirred up, so the letters are agitated into a new order

annotation.surface: A hot tub with two men in it sets a small chap aflutter.
annotation.walkthrough: Tom Thumb is the thumb-sized hero of an English folk tale.
annotation.definitionFit: Tom Thumb, no bigger than a thumb, is the archetypal little fellow.

entries.clue: Send fresh fish minus tail for broadcaster (3,7)

indicatorNotes.fresh: made anew, so the letters are reworked
indicatorNotes.minus tail: a fish's tail is its end, so without it the word loses its last letter

annotation.surface: An instruction to dispatch fish, tail removed, to a presenter.
annotation.walkthrough: Ned Sherrin was a British broadcaster and producer, host of Radio 4's Loose Ends and producer of That Was The Week That Was.
annotation.definitionFit: Ned Sherrin presented radio and television programmes for decades.

entries.clue: Eliot’s cruellest month lands pair in trouble (5)

blocks.note: surface padding: it only lands the pair in trouble

annotation.surface: A spring month in which a couple get into difficulties.
annotation.walkthrough: The Waste Land by T S Eliot opens 'April is the cruellest month'.
annotation.definitionFit: Eliot named April as the cruellest month in the first line of The Waste Land.

entries.clue: City area veto damaged union privilege (5,4)

indicatorNotes.damaged: knocked out of shape, so the letters change order

annotation.surface: A council ban in some district harms the rights of a trade union.
annotation.walkthrough: A block vote lets a trade union cast all its members' votes as one, a power it has held at Labour Party conferences.
annotation.definitionFit: The block vote is a voting right exercised by a trade union on behalf of its members.

entries.clue: Dramatist jokes amongst current company (7)

indicatorNotes.amongst: placed in the middle of other letters

blocks.note: 'that's a good one' — a one is a joke

annotation.surface: A playwright's humour goes down well with a theatre company of the day.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Current company' reads as a present-day troupe; it is two abbreviations, I and CO, with ONES tucked between. Eugène Ionesco wrote absurdist plays such as Rhinoceros.
annotation.definitionFit: Eugène Ionesco was a Romanian-French dramatist.

entries.clue: Understatement from one devoured by 50 bears? (7)

blocks.note: to tote = to carry, to bear

annotation.surface: Saying fifty bears ate someone would be an understatement, the question mark admits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bears' is not the animals but a verb, carries; I goes inside L+TOTES. Litotes is understatement by negation: 'not bad' for good.
annotation.definitionFit: Litotes is the figure of speech that makes a point by understating it.

entries.clue: European republic in revolution inspiring unease (5)

annotation.surface: A European state in the grip of a revolt causes anxiety.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In revolution' suggests political upheaval; it only means turn round. Eire is the Irish name for the Republic of Ireland.
annotation.definitionFit: Something eerie is strange in a way that makes one uneasy.

entries.clue: Where daddy treated murderous alter ego (6,4)

indicatorNotes.treated: processed, so the letters are worked into a new order

annotation.surface: A question about where a father took a killer's other self for a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: Mr Edward Hyde is the murderous other self of Dr Jekyll in Stevenson's novella.
annotation.definitionFit: Hyde is the alter ego Dr Jekyll turns into, and he commits murder.

entries.clue: Duck in city by river and building thereon (9)

indicatorNotes.by: beside, so the pieces sit next to each other

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O
the Ouse, a river in England

annotation.surface: A duck sits in town by the water, near a building on the bank.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thereon' points back to the river in the wordplay: the definition leans on the rest of the clue. A duck in cricket is a score of zero.
annotation.definitionFit: A boathouse is a building on a river, where boats are kept.

entries.clue: Fanatical sort in old car following van (10)

indicatorNotes.following: comes after, so this piece goes second

blocks.note: the van (vanguard) is the head, the front
a banger is a battered old car

annotation.surface: A zealot is riding in an old car behind a van.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Van' is the vehicle in the surface, but it means the front, as in vanguard. A banger is British slang for a clapped-out car.
annotation.definitionFit: A headbanger is a wild-eyed zealot, a fanatic.

entries.clue: Nimble Warwick is strangely optimistic character (7,8)

indicatorNotes.strangely: oddly arranged, so the letters are reordered

annotation.surface: A person called Warwick, quick on his feet, is an odd kind of cheerful figure.
annotation.walkthrough: Wilkins Micawber in Dickens's David Copperfield is forever sure that 'something will turn up'.
annotation.definitionFit: Mr Micawber is literature's byword for hopeless optimism.

entries.clue: Syrian neighbour curses in shelter (8)

blocks.note: the lee is the sheltered side

annotation.surface: Someone next door to Syria swears as they take cover.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Curses' reads as swearing; it is a noun, banes.
annotation.definitionFit: Lebanon borders Syria, so a Lebanese person is a Syrian's neighbour.

entries.clue: Stakes raised for the defence? (8)

blocks.note: not bets increased, but wooden posts stood upright in a row
not a lawyer's case, but protection against attack; the question mark flags the double reading

annotation.surface: A gambler, or a lawyer, ups the stakes to help the defence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stakes raised' sounds like a bigger bet and 'the defence' like a court case; literally they are posts stood upright to keep attackers out.
annotation.definitionFit: A stockade is a barrier of upright stakes put up for defence.

entries.clue: Outlaw cross about wine store next to house (5,4)

indicatorNotes.about: around, so the cross wraps what follows
indicatorNotes.next to: beside, so the two pieces are joined

blocks.note: a rood is a cross, as in rood screen
a wine bin, a rack for storing bottles

annotation.surface: A bandit, angered by a cellar beside a home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry, but it is the noun: a rood is the cross in a church. A wine bin is a rack for bottles.
annotation.definitionFit: Robin Hood is the legendary outlaw of Sherwood Forest.

entries.clue: Period outside court on left foot (6)

indicatorNotes.on: attached to, so the next piece is added

blocks.note: a day is a period of time

annotation.surface: A time of standing outside the court on one's left foot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Foot' is the metrical kind, not the one you stand on.
annotation.definitionFit: A dactyl is a metrical foot of one stressed and two unstressed syllables.

entries.clue: Romantic writer in past first to leave club (5)

indicatorNotes.first to leave: the first letter is the one that walks out, as a member leaves a club

blocks.note: to go by = to go past
a golf club, IRON, loses its first letter

annotation.surface: A poet of the Romantic era once gave up his club membership.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Club' reads as a society to be left; it is a golf club, IRON.
annotation.definitionFit: Lord Byron was one of the great English Romantic poets.

entries.clue: Attacker, one helping to support Resistance (6)

indicatorNotes.to support: in a down clue, a supporter sits underneath

annotation.surface: An assailant, an ally who backs the wartime Resistance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Resistance' has the wartime movement in mind; it is simply R. In a down entry what supports comes below.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one who makes a raid is an attacker.

entries.clue: Bully ambassador parking in constricted space (7)

blocks.note: HE = His Excellency, an ambassador's title
a neck is a narrow passage, as of a bottle

annotation.surface: An envoy is harassed about parking in a tight spot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bully' looks like a noun but the answer is a verb: to henpeck is to nag and domineer.
annotation.definitionFit: To henpeck someone, usually a husband, is to bully them with constant nagging.

entries.clue: Value reflected welcoming a wronged brother (4)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: taking in, so it wraps what follows

blocks.note: use = value, as in 'of little use'

annotation.surface: Thinking over what a mistreated sibling was worth.
annotation.walkthrough: Esau, in Genesis, was cheated of his birthright and blessing by his twin brother Jacob.
annotation.definitionFit: Esau was wronged by his brother Jacob, who took his blessing.

entries.clue: Satire performed – stick around (7)

indicatorNotes.around: wraps round the piece before it

annotation.surface: A satirical piece is staged with a walking stick as a prop.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash suggests a stage direction; 'around' at the end tells the stick to wrap what comes before it. Candide is Voltaire's 1759 satire.
annotation.definitionFit: Candide is Voltaire's satire on philosophical optimism.

entries.clue: Scratching head, Kerouac and Ginsberg scoff (4)

indicatorNotes.Scratching head: the head, first letter, is struck out

blocks.note: Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg were Beat writers, BEATS; drop the B

annotation.surface: Two puzzled Beat poets sneer at something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' looks like mockery, which suits the poets; it is the British slang sense, to eat greedily.
annotation.definitionFit: To scoff is to eat hungrily, so he scoffs = he eats.

entries.clue: Despicable celeb in pop lady cleaned out (9)

indicatorNotes.cleaned out: emptied of the middle, leaving the outer letters

annotation.surface: A contemptible celebrity featured in a pop song about a woman down on her luck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pop' tempts as music, beside 'celeb'; it is a father, DAD.
annotation.definitionFit: Dastardly means wicked and contemptible.

entries.clue: Put out in Paris, I recalled shocking treatment (5)

annotation.surface: Someone upset in Paris remembers harsh treatment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shocking' sounds like outrage; it is literal, the electric-shock therapy ECT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to put out a troublemaker is to throw them out.
